Velvet Ants of Louisiana

Interactive dichotomous key — answer questions step by step to identify any velvet ant you encounter

Identify Your Velvet Ant

This key guides you through a series of binary choices — each question narrows down the possibilities until you reach a species identification. This guide covers 13 velvet ants (family Mutillidae) recorded in Louisiana, from the large, unmistakable Eastern Velvet Ant ("cow killer") down to several small, easily-confused Dasymutilla, Pseudomethoca, and Timulla species. Velvet ants are actually solitary wasps, not true ants — the wingless, ant-mimicking females pictured throughout this key are the form most people encounter running across open ground; males are fully winged, look like an entirely different insect, and cannot sting.

Handle with care: female velvet ants deliver one of the most painful defensive stings of any North American insect, though they are not aggressive and sting only when handled, stepped on, or squeezed. Several genera here — especially the three black-and-white banded Timulla and the plain rust-colored Dasymutilla trio (Bear, Scarlet, and Two-spotted Velvet Ants) — are genuinely difficult to separate from a photo alone and are sometimes only confirmed by an expert.
